title: They Got the Lights Back. They Did Not Get the Propeller Back.
title_candidates: They Got the Lights Back. They Did Not Get the Propeller Back.
Sixty-Seven Seconds From the Order to the River.
Eight People Were Filling Potholes on the Key Bridge.
description:
At twenty-seven minutes and fifty-three seconds past one in the morning, a duty officer in Baltimore gave an order to stop the traffic. Sixty-seven seconds later the bridge was in the river, and six men who had been filling potholes on it were gone.

Eight people were up there — a seven-person road maintenance crew and one inspector. Below them, at the Seagirt Marine Terminal, a container ship was finishing her cargo. She was called the Dali. She flew the flag of Singapore, and her international number was 9697428. She was loaded, and she was bound for Sri Lanka.

This is a film about the four minutes between those two facts, and about why every lever anyone reached for moved something other than the ship.

At about seven minutes past one, once she was in the channel, the tugboats let go. That is normal. Every night. Every port. At about twenty-five minutes past one, she was six tenths of a mile out. And the lights went out. Two electrical breakers — HR1 and LR1 — opened without being told to. She lost her lighting. She lost the pumps that cooled the main engine. She lost the pumps that moved the steering gear. The crew closed those breakers by hand and the power came back. Two tenths of a mile from the bridge it happened again, and this time the generators came off the high-voltage bus entirely.

The pilots called for a tug within seventy-four seconds of the first blackout. The Eric McAllister answered immediately and turned toward them; she was three miles away and she never reached the ship. The pilots' dispatcher called the Coast Guard. A pilot broadcast a warning to everything floating in the Patapsco. The duty officer stopped the traffic. Thirty-one seconds after the second blackout the crew closed two different breakers by hand and got the lights back — and they got the electricity back before the ship touched the bridge. They did not get the propeller back.

On the eighteenth of November, 2025, the National Transportation Safety Board met and determined the probable cause: a loose signal wire connection to a terminal block, stemming from the improper installation of wire-label banding, which caused the loss of electrical power, which caused the loss of propulsion and steering close to the bridge. A band of labelling around a wire had stopped it seating fully into a spring-clamp gate.

The Board also found that contributing to the collapse and to the loss of life was the absence of countermeasures to reduce the bridge's vulnerability to being struck by an ocean-going vessel — countermeasures that could have been put in place if the Maryland Transportation Authority had carried out a vulnerability assessment. It did not find that Maryland knew and ignored the risk. It found that they were likely unaware. On the twentieth of March, 2025, the Board named sixty-eight bridges in the United States for which it recommended a vulnerability evaluation.

Six days after the collapse, on the first of April, 2024, the ship's owner and manager filed in the District of Maryland for exoneration from, or limitation of, liability, asking to be capped at about forty-three point seven million dollars. The United States put in a claim of one hundred and three million, seventy-eight thousand and fifty-six dollars. The companies agreed to pay one hundred and one million, nine hundred and eighty thousand dollars. That is a settlement of a civil claim. It is not an admission of anything, and it is not a criminal finding.

On the twelfth of May, 2026, a federal court in Maryland unsealed an indictment. An indictment is merely an accusation, and all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Those are the Department of Justice's own words, and this programme holds to them: three defendants stand charged, two companies and one man, and none of them has been tried or convicted of anything.

Every light in this story came back on. That was never the thing that had to hold.

—

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. Sources for this episode are the National Transportation Safety Board's board meeting of 18 November 2025, the indictment unsealed 12 May 2026, and the limitation proceeding in the District of Maryland.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
